entries.title: Iran: Trump says strikes unlikely if peace talks keep moving
entries.summary: After weeks of rumors that the US and Israel were preparing new strikes on Iran, President Donald Trump said it was "highly unlikely" that he would order a new escalation as the Iranians "want to make a deal so badly."
entries.content:
Iran

Iran: Trump says strikes unlikely if peace talks keep moving

November 8, 2026

After weeks of rumors that the US and Israel were preparing new strikes on Iran, President Donald Trump said it was "highly unlikely" that he would order a new escalation as the Iranians "want to make a deal so badly."

In an interview with US broadcaster CNN, President Donald Trump sought to downplay fears that the US is about to relaunch its military campaign against Iran.

"It depends on whether or not they sign a very strong agreement," he told CNN on Sunday. "The answer is highly unlikely it's going to be necessary."

At the same time, Trump restated that the US military was "ready" to launch a new round of strikes and could "finish [Iran] off."

"I've got three aircraft carriers here," he said. "They're fully locked and loaded."

He added that the US military had 38 bridges in their sights "that we can knock down in literally one hour."

However, Trump also repeated several times that the new escalation is "highly unlikely," saying that Iran was a "failing nation" and "withering away financially" after eight months of hostilities.

"I hit them so hard. You don't know how hard I hit them," he said. "They want to make a deal so badly."

Iran and the US stuck between war and peace

Trump ordered an attack on Iran in late February, after US ally Israel launched what it called a "preemptive strike" on its biggest regional rival. The US president has since repeatedly declared victory, insinuated that Iran was begging the US for a deal, and told the media that a peace deal was done or nearly done.

Iran has repeatedly rejected Trump's account. Despite Trump's claims that Iran was collapsing both economically and militarily, Tehran has been able to repeatedly stage attacks on US allies in the region and maintains at least a partial blockade of the Strait of Hormuz. The Houthi rebels in Yemen, allied with Tehran, are currently targeting high-profile targets in the Saudi capital of Riyadh and elsewhere across Saudi Arabia.

The most tangible diplomatic achievement since the start of the war was reported in June, when Iran and the US signed a memorandum of understanding in Islamabad. But the talks broke down and the memorandum expired in August​​​​​​​, with the two sides still engaged in a military and diplomatic stalemate.

Iranian top diplomat says US still digesting midterms

The conflict has proven to be unpopular with the US public, featuring heavily in the campaign for US midterm election that eventually saw Trump's Republicans lose their majorities in Congress.

On Sunday, Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said that that peace mediators did not "travel" since the Tuesday election in the US. Araghchi described the outcome as a "shock."

"We now have to see how long it will take for them to digest these results, in order to determine how we are going to move forward," he said.

Qatar says talks moving behind the scenes

Qatar, which acts as one of the mediators in the conflict, denied rumors that the US and Iran are failing to reach a peace deal. On Saturday, the Qatari prime minister said both sides were still working toward an agreement.

Separately, the Reuters news agency cited a senior Iranian official as saying that Tehran has submitted a proposal on its nuclear program to Washington through Qatar.

The official also noted that further talks would depend on the US meeting Tehran's demands, including the lifting of sanctions, unfreezing Iranian funds and war reparations.

entries.title: Germany news: Merz to nominate Aigner for president
entries.summary: German Chancellor Friedrich Merz announced that he will nominate Ilse Aigner for federal president, paving the way for her to be the first woman to hold the office. DW has more.
entries.content:
Germany

Germany news: Merz to nominate Aigner for president

Published November 7, 2026last updated November 8, 2026

German Chancellor Friedrich Merz announced that he will nominate Ilse Aigner for federal president, paving the way for her to be the first woman to hold the office. DW has more.

Skip next section What you need to know

What you need to know

  • German Chancellor Friedrich Merz confirmed he will nominate Ilse Aigner for president
  • Iranian opposition politician Reza Pahlavi accepted a 'Freedom Prize' in Frankfurt
  • More than 18,000 people rallied to show support for Pahlavi, but some others protested
  • Man replaced the German flag with a Palestinian one at the Berlin parliament building

This is a roundup of the top stories from and about Germany on the weekend of Saturday, November 7, and Sunday, November 8, 2026:

Skip next section Merz to nominate Aigner as Germany's next federal president

Merz to nominate Aigner as Germany's next federal president

German Chancellor Friedrich Merz announced to the Christian Democrat Union (CDU) party heads his intention to nominate Ilse Aigner as the country's next federal president, according to the dpa, AFP and Reuters news agencies.

She will replace Frank-Walter Steinmeier when he steps down at the end of his term early next year.

Aigner, who hails from Bavaria's conservative Christian Social Union (CSU) and is the president of the Bavarian state parliament, would be the first woman to hold the German president's position should she be elected on January 30. 

Steinmeier is a member of the junior coalition partner SPD.

Merz will officially pitch Aigner's name for the job on Monday, when party leaders will gather to choose a joint candidate.

SPD and Green Party representatives have already voiced support for her candidacy.

Skip next section Russia officially unveils plaque honoring East German spymaster who brought down Willy Brandt

Russia officially unveils plaque honoring East German spymaster who brought down Willy Brandt

The city of Moscow has officially unveiled a new commemorative plaque honoring one of communist East Germany's top Cold War spies, Markus Wolf.

The plaque was initially installed by Russia's Foreign Intelligence Service (SVR) at Nizhny Kislovsky Lane 8 in September to mark the site where Wolf and his family, who were religious Jews and communists, lived between 1934 and 1945 after fleeing Nazi Germany.

Wolf would go on to spend nearly 30 years at the top of the foreign department of East Germany's Ministry for State Security, or Stasi, and was considered one of the Cold War's ultimate spymasters.

The spymaster was long known as "the man without a face" by Western intelligence services because they had no idea what he looked like.

Wolf's ability to place agent Günter Guillaume within West German Chancellor Willy Brandt's inner circle, ultimately leading to Brandt's 1974 resignation, is considered to be one of his greatest successes.

Wolf's widow Andrea reportedly expressed her gratitude for the honor in a letter addressed to "all Russian friends." Wolf died in Berlin on November 9, 2006, at the age of 83.

Skip next section Body of missing 13-year-old Berlin girl found in abandoned house, suspect in custody

Body of missing 13-year-old Berlin girl found in abandoned house, suspect in custody

The Berlin Police and the Berlin Public Prosecutor's Office on Sunday evening issued a joint statement announcing that they believe that a body found in an abandoned house in Brandenburg is in fact that of Lisa T., a 13-year-old Berlin girl who went missing on her way to school Tuesday morning.

Police in Brandenburg found the body, as well as an injured male whom they believe to be responsible for the child's death, when they acted on a tip from locals alerting them of a break-in.

Authorities say the man is in critical condition at a nearby hospital where he is under police guard. Further, authorities say the man's injuries were self-induced.

Police are now working to ascertain the man's identity.

On Friday, the police said that the girl had likely not disappeared voluntarily. On Saturday, they said that it must be assumed that she had been the victim of a crime.

Skip next section Bundesliga: FC Bayern's woes continue as Neuer goes down to injury

Bundesliga: FC Bayern's woes continue as Neuer goes down to injury

Veteran keeper Manuel Neuer has been added to the list of walking wounded at Bundesliga top team FC Bayern Munich, suffering a torn foot tendon in his team's 2-1 victory in Mainz.

Neuer, who posted on social media that "an injury never comes at the right time, but it's part of the game," left the match just before the half.

Bayern released a statement saying that the champion goalie would be "out for the time being."

Though no further information was given, media reports suggested Neuer could be out for at least two months.

"I've been through this before, and I'll get through this one, too," said Neuer. "From now on: full focus on recovery. Until then, I will support the boys on the pitch wherever I can."

A two-time Champions League winner, Neuer made club history at the start of the match — his 550th in Germany's Bundesliga — as the oldest ever player to take the pitch for Bayern at age 40 years and 225 days.

The veteran's absence will only compound Bayern's injury woes as they battle on without head coach Vincent Kompany — who is recovering from an illness — as well as Jamal Musiala, Luis Diaz, Ismael Saibari and Serge Gnabry — all of whom are on long-term injured reserve.

Skip next section German citizen among 15 wounded in Krakow shooting, Steinmeier voices solidarity

German citizen among 15 wounded in Krakow shooting, Steinmeier voices solidarity

As authorities in Poland try to make sense of yesterday's deadly shooting in Krakow, lists of victims' nationalities have been made public. 

Of the six victims shot and killed at the city's market square on Saturday, four were women and two were men. Three of the women and one of the men were Polish, while the remaining woman was from Austria and the man from the UK.

Austrian, British, German, Portuguese and Russian passport holders were among the 15 individuals wounded by the Polish gunman.

German Federal President Frank-Walter Steinmeier's office on Sunday posted a statement of support on X, writing: "In this difficult hour, Germany stands in mourning and solidarity with Poland and its citizens."

Further, Steinmeier expressed his condolences to Polish President Karol Nawocki, saying, "my thoughts are with the victims and their families."

Skip next section Allgäu Alps lose their lost glacier, researchers say

Allgäu Alps lose their lost glacier, researchers say

Researchers have confirmed the loss of the Schwarzmilzferner, the last glacier in the Allgäu Alps on the border between Germany and Austria.

Estimates by researchers say that the eastern Alps could be completely ice-free by 2070 due to climate change and rising global temperatures.

The glacier was located on the Austrian side of the mountain range at an altitude of 2,450 meters (8038 feet).

It can no longer be considered a glacier as it has lost over 4 meters in thickness and around half its volume earlier this year, glaciologist Cristoph Mayer told the dpa news agency.

Mayer said that the glacier will likely disappear "completely" by next summer.

The rapid melting came as Europe was hit by a massive heatwave over the summer of 2026.

"Even if there is heavy snowfall in winter, the ice masses are shrinking rapidly. Summers have now become too hot for them," Mayer said.

"As things stand, I expect the entire Eastern Alps to be ice-free between 2060 and 2070."

Skip next section Man replaces German flag with Palestinian flag at Berlin parliament building

Man replaces German flag with Palestinian flag at Berlin parliament building

A 22-year-old man took down the German flag at the Reichstag building in Berlin and replaced it with a Palestinian flag, police said on Sunday.

The Reichstag building is the seat of the lower house of German parliament, the Bundestag. The large German flag that flies in front of the building is known as the Unity Flag, or Flagge der Einheit in German, as it commemorates the German reunification of 1990.

The man climbed up the flagpole using a climbing harness at around 11:30 a.m. local time (1030 UTC) and threw the German flag to the ground, police said.

He lowered himself back down on his own, according to police, after which he was taken into custody.

He was supported by two other men aged 20 and 32, according to the report.

Police have launched an investigation into a suspected case of denigration of the state and its symbols, damaging public property and trespassing.

The Palestinian flag was removed with the assistance of the fire department.

As the mast hoisting cable had been damaged in the incident, the German flag could not be immediately raised again.

Skip next section Camel survives collision with bus in Bavaria

Camel survives collision with bus in Bavaria

A camel survived a collision with a bus in southern Germany.

The accident occurred on a rural road in Riedering, a town southeast of Munich in the state of Bavaria.

According to police, three camels escaped a fenced pasture, with one of them ending up on the road on which the accident occurred when the bus drove past it at 8am local time.

While the camel did not sustain any injuries, the bus suffered an estimated €500 ($552) worth of damage.

Skip next section Bavaria's Söder calls for return to conscription

Bavaria's Söder calls for return to conscription

Bavarian Premier Markus Söder has spoken out in favor of military conscription in remarks seemingly in response to Defense Minister Boris Pistorius, who this week said he believed the draft was not necessary in the near future (see earlier entry in this blog).

"If our democracy is important to us, we have to stand up for it. That's why it is clear: We need true military conscription again," he wrote on X.

"Germany is threatened in a way it has not been in a long time," Söder wrote. "That is why we have to keep strengthening the Bundeswehr."

Söder, who also leads the conservative Christian Social Union (CSU), which forms part of Germany's coalition government, said the current large investments in equipment and infrastructure were not enough on their own.

"A new concept of defense for the country and its allies also needs more soldiers," he wrote.

In remarks published on Saturday, Pistorius told newspapers from the Funke media group that the Bundeswehr currently had some 190,000 members, the highest level in 13 years, meaning that voluntary recruitment measures were working.

"If this trajectory continues, we will have no problems with growth," he said, and there would not have to be "a discussion about conscription of whatever kind."

During Gen Z protests last weekend, young demonstrators called among other things for an end to any considerations of reintroducing military conscription. 

Skip next section IG Metall union calls for strike at Mercedes-Benz plant

IG Metall union calls for strike at Mercedes-Benz plant

Germany's largest union, IG Metall, has called on workers at a Mercedes-Benz plant outside Berlin to walk out for two hours on Monday amid stalled wage negotiations.

Employees at local car supplier Gestamp in Ludwigsfelde, a town south of Berlin, have also been called upon to take part in the industrial action.

IG Metall is demanding 5% more pay for the around 96,000 employees in the metal and electrical industry in the states of Berlin and Brandenburg as part of a 12-month collective wage agreement, as well as job and location security.

The strike is being called after the union failed to reach agreement in a third round of a wage dispute.

During a second round of talks, the employers presented a coordinated nationwide offer of a one-off payment next year and a 1.3% pay rise in July 2028, which was rejected by the union as inadequate.

Skip next section Holocaust denial on the up among young people — Anne Frank Zentrum

Holocaust denial on the up among young people — Anne Frank Zentrum

Young people are increasingly denying the facts of the Holocaust or downplaying its horrors, according to the head of the Anne Frank Zentrum in Berlin.

In remarks made to the Catholic news agency KNA ahead of the 88th anniversary of the November pogroms in Germany, Veronika Nahm said that people attending traveling exhibitions organized by the center sometimes asked, "Is that even true?"

She said that people downplaying or denying the Holocaust was particularly apparent in social media posts connected with the center.

She said there were comments such as, "Why do you commemorate Anne Frank, why not a child in Gaza?"

Lack of information, not bad intentions

Nahm attributes the rise in such opinions to ignorance rather than bad intentions on the part of young people, saying they were not as well-informed on the topic in schools as they were 15 years ago.

"There has been a generational change of teachers. For many older teachers, it was close to their hearts, and it was mentioned in many places and subjects during lessons. That is different today," she said.

Nahm said it was important that visits by young people to sites commemorating the Holocaust be used to strengthen their feeling of empathy, something that worked particularly well with the story of Anne Frank.

The Anne Frank Zentrum in Berlin is a partner organization to the Anne Frank House in Amsterdam.

Anne Frank was a Jewish girl who hid in that house during the 1940-1945 German occupation of the Netherlands and wrote a famous diary, later published, about her experiences and feelings.

She was discovered and deported by the Nazis and died in the Bergen-Belsen concentration camp in early 1945.

The November pogroms, during which Jews and Jewish property and institutions were attacked, took place on November 9-10, 1938, across the German Reich at the instigation of Germany's Nazi regime.

Skip next section Large majority for fuel price cap, windfall tax — survey

Large majority for fuel price cap, windfall tax — survey

Most people in Germany favor the government imposing a cap on prices for gasoline and diesel, a survey has shown.

The government is currently debating such a cap, which would replace a current fuel tax rebate that runs out at the end of the year.

According to the survey by the NIM Institute, 71% of the people asked said they would like the government to control fuel prices.

Altogether 66% of respondents were in favor of levying a windfall tax on oil corporations, which have been turning in massive profits amid shortages caused largely by the war in Iran.

Other measures to relieve the pressure on motorists amid surging fuel prices were less popular, according to the survey.

Just 56% of respondents wanted to see a rise in the allowed tax deduction for commuters, and just 52% favored direct payments from the state to drivers on low incomes.

Skip next section Enviroment minister hopes for progress at UN climate conference

Enviroment minister hopes for progress at UN climate conference

German Environment Minister Carsten Schneider has said he hopes agreement will be reached on measures to limit global warming at the UN Climate Change Conference over the next two weeks.

"The faster global emissions fall, the faster we can bring the temperature curve back down to 1.5 degrees Celsius (2.7 degrees Fahrenheit). At the same time, we must do more to protect people from the effects of heat waves, droughts and floods," Schneider said.

Schneider was referring to the target of limiting global warming to 1.5 C compared with pre-industrial levels agreed on under the Paris climate accords.

The UN said last month, however, that this target will be missed within the century, with most nations failing to reduce their greenhouse gas emissions by a significant amount.

Schneider also said moving toward electricity as the main source of energy was the best way to combat climate change, which is being driven largely by the human burning of fossil fuels such as oil and gas.

Merz announces his absence

Schneider will be the only German Cabinet member to attend the  COP31 summit, which kicks off in Turkey on Monday.

Chancellor Friedrich Merz has decided to skip the event, citing "other commitments."

His decision has drawn considerable criticism, with leading German climate activist Luisa Neubauer saying it sent "the worst possible signal to the international community."

"It is unworthy of Germany and an insult, particularly to those nations around the world that are already facing an existential threat from rising sea levels," she said.

Media reports say Merz is planning a visit to an Italian restaurant with his wife and daughter for his 71st birthday on Wednesday while the summit is underway, leading Neubauer to describe his non-appearance as a "Bella Italia absence."

Nearly 200 states will convene for the summit in Antalya.

Skip next section Search continues for missing 13-year-old girl in Berlin

Search continues for missing 13-year-old girl in Berlin

Police in Berlin are still looking for a 13-year-old girl who disappeared on the way to school on Tuesday.

In a statement, Berlin police said they could not rule out that the girl, who has been identified as Lisa T., "has been the victim of a crime."

"Based on the current state of the investigation, it is assumed that the child did not leave her home environment voluntarily," police said.

Around 220 police officers were deployed in the Marzahn district of the German capital on Saturday, with a police spokesman saying that the search was time-consuming because of the large number of houses and parks in the area.

The search began on Friday, supported by sniffer dogs and a police helicopter.

Skip next section Pay gap narrows for women executives

Pay gap narrows for women executives

Women on the executive boards of Germany's leading listed companies were earning almost as much on average as their male colleagues in 2025, a study by consultancy EY says.

According to the study, female board members at companies listed on the DAX, MDAX and SDAX indices, not including chief executives, earned an average of €2.20 million ($2.45 million) last year.

That is a rise of 2.4% from 2024.

Their male counterparts, on the other hand, saw a nearly 2% reduction in their pay down to €2.23 million, which reduced the pay gap from €121,000 to €26,000.

The study also found that there were more women serving on executive boards in 2025 than a year previously, with 101 female board members compared with 88 in 2024 and just 33 in 2013.

"Women on executive boards are no longer the exception. That is also reflected in salaries," said EY partner Jens Massmann.

entries.title: Many killed after migrant boat sinks off Senegal
entries.summary: The incident occurred near Kebemer off the coast of northwestern Senegal. Authorities on El Hierro in the Canary Islands have declared an emergency after a marked increase in migrant boat arrivals.
entries.content:
Senegal

Many killed after migrant boat sinks off Senegal

November 8, 2026

The incident occurred near Kebemer off the coast of northwestern Senegal. Authorities on El Hierro in the Canary Islands have declared an emergency after a marked increase in migrant boat arrivals.

At least 34 people were killed after a small boat carrying migrants sank off the coast of northwestern Senegal, according to the Senegalese Press Agency.

Thousands have died in recent years after embarking on boats from the Senegalese coast in order to reach Spain's Canary Islands through the perilous Atlantic route.

Initially, the Senegalese Ministry of the Interior stated that only one person had been rescued from the capsizing and that 21 bodies had been recovered.

The ministry added that the toll was "provisional" and that search operations were still ongoing.

The incident occurred near Kebemer, some 180 kilometers (around 112 miles) north of the capital, Dakar.

On Saturday, the ministry stressed the government's "determination to combat people smuggling networks, notably through strengthened cooperation with neighboring countries."

Senegalese authorities said they intercepted 142 migrants on a similar boat aimed at reaching Spanish territory on Friday. The boat included nationals of multiple West African countries.

El Hierro island declares emergency over migrant arrivals

Authorities on El Hierro Island in the Canary Islands declared an emergency on Saturday after a marked increase in migrant boat arrivals.

El Hierro officials say that over 3,300 people have arrived on around 30 boats since the start of the month.

"We are very concerned... by this sharp increase in arrivals," Alpidio Armas, head of the El Hierro regional council, told Spanish television.

"This is precisely what has led us to declare an emergency in order to ensure a framework of cooperation with higher-level institutions," he added.

Armas said that conditions at the island's hospital have become "undesirable."

El Hierro is home to about 11,400 residents.

Migrant arrivals reached a record high of 46,000 in 2024. Afterwards, arrivals have fallen sharply due to increased surveillance and cooperation with African countries.

entries.title: South Africa elections: ANC marks its worst-ever performance
entries.summary: The African National Congress, the party of late Nobel Prize winner Nelson Mandela, slumped to its worst-ever result in South Africa's municipal election. The voters blame the ANC for water and electricity shortages.
entries.content:
South Africa

South Africa's ANC hit by worst-ever performance in local elections

November 8, 2026

The African National Congress, the party of late Nobel Prize winner Nelson Mandela, slumped to its worst-ever result in South Africa's municipal election. The voters blame the ANC for water and electricity shortages.

South Africa's African National Congress (ANC) turned in a historically poor election performance, with the the final tally published on Sunday giving them less than 31% of the vote in Wednesday's municipal polls.

Their closes rival, the Democratic Alliance (DA), won just under 25% of the vote.

The ANC also lost its majority in six of the eight metropolitan regions, South Africa's Electoral Commission said on Saturday. With no outright winner declared in several major cities, politicians are expected enter tough coalition talks to form municipal governments. 

ANC secretary general says outcome 'catastrophic'

While the ANC remains the most popular party in the country, they have been struggling with growing backlash from voters. In 2026, many South Africans are frustrated by water and electricity shortages, with the ANC taking the blame for the poor state of municipalities.  High unemployment, crime, and widespread corruption are high on the public agenda.

ANC leader, and South African president, Cyril Ramaphosa, has not yet addressed his party's poor performance. In his weekly presidential letter, however, he admitted that "municipal failures have contributed to declining public trust and confidence in democratic governance." 

On Saturday, ANC Secretary-General Fikile Mbalula told reporters that the ANC needs to work on winning back public confidence.

"We cannot ask the people to trust us merely because of our history," Mbalula said.

"This has been a very catastrophic outcome for the ANC ... as much as we are the largest party, it has been catastrophic for the movement," he added.

The ANC's steady decline with voters

The ANC had governed with an absolute majority for most of its history up until the general election in 2024 saw it lose an outright parliamentary majority for the first time in South Africa's democratic era.

"This is the most severe result that the ANC would have feared," political analyst Daniel Silke told the AFP news agency.

"It's the ANC's worst result in history," Silke said, adding that the result will undermine the ANC's ability to exert authority on the local and national level. The results could also provide a bellwether of voter sentiment ahead of the 2029 general elections.

Once led by Nelson Mandela, the ANC was instrumental in ending apartheid, and took and power in 1994 after South Africa became a democracy.

But over the past decade, it has steadily performed worse in one election after another. In 2024, the ANC secured just over 40% in the 2024 national polls and 46% at the previous municipal elections in 2021.

After losing the absolute majority in 2024, the ANC formed a cross-party national unity government with all the parties represented in parliament, which is still in power.

The ANC's decline comes amid disillusionment over corruption, mismanagement and high unemployment. Smaller parties have also emerged across South Africa's political landscape, cutting into the ANC's voter base.

DA opposition holds large cities

The pro-business, center-right DA is set to keep control of Cape Town after winning an absolute majority. It also performed well in the capital, Pretoria, and economic hub of Johannesburg, and is expected to form coalitions that exclude the ANC.

"All of the cut and thrust that comes with the election is now over, and it is time now... to put together governments that can actually fix these towns and cities," DA leader Geordin Hill-Lewis told reporters.

"We have already reached out to many parties over the last 24 hours and will continue to do so today," he said.

entries.title: Egypt train crash leaves several dead, over 100 injured
entries.summary: A train derailed after colliding with another train south of Cairo, with authorities confirming several deaths and saying more than 100 passengers were injured. Over 50 ambulances were deployed to the scene.
entries.content:
Egypt

Egypt train crash leaves several dead, over 100 injured

November 8, 2026

A train derailed after colliding with another train south of Cairo, with authorities confirming several deaths and saying more than 100 passengers were injured. Over 50 ambulances were deployed to the scene.

At least seven people were killed in the train collision in Egypt on Sunday, with authorities also confirming over 100 people were injured.

The collision involved one train hitting the rear end of another while traveling through the Giza province on the line between Cairo and the southern Nile city of Aswan. One of the trains then derailed and several cars flipped, according to the Egyptian authorities.

Officials said 52 ambulances were deployed to the scene some 52 kilometers (32 miles) south of Cairo. Emergency crews and cranes were also working to clear the line and restore railway traffic through Giza's al-Ayyat district.

The cause of the accident was not immediately clear.

El-Sissi says incident being investigated

In a social media post, Egyptian President Abdel-Fattah el-Sissi said he ordered an investigation. He also urged the state agencies to "hold accountable anyone found to have been negligent."

The crash tool place in the same area as the worst train disaster in Egypt's history, which saw over 370 people were killed in a train fire in 2002. Several crashes also claimed dozens of lives in the same region in 2009.

In recent years, Egypt has invested billions of dollars into new highways and high-speed rail lines, but is still facing safety issues and repeated crashes while attempting to revamp its aging rail network.

entries.title: Israel: Eisenkot officially tasked with forming a government
entries.summary: Israeli President Isaac Herzog tasked Gadi Eisenkot with the right of trying to form a government. The opposition leader's way to replacing Benjamin Netanyahu as prime minister is full of political challenges.
entries.content:
Israel

Israel: Eisenkot officially tasked with forming a government

November 8, 2026

Israeli President Isaac Herzog tasked Gadi Eisenkot with the right of trying to form a government. The opposition leader's way to replacing Benjamin Netanyahu as prime minister is full of political challenges.

Israel President Isaac Herzog has officially tasked Gadi Eisenkot with forming a government.

Eisenkot, the head of the centrist Yashar party, will have 28 days to secure a coalition to replace current Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's religious-nationalist government, with Herzog having the authority to prolong Eisenkot's mandate by 14 days.

"The conversations with the different parties were open and transparent, while also resurfacing the many voices in Israeli society. They reminded us the fact that all Israeli citizens have an equal voice, from all parts of society," Herzog said.

He stressed that Eisenkot received the clearest support from the majority of Knesset members when it comes to the question of forming the next government.

"The challenges we face are giant. Iran is not waiting a second in its threats. We have to start building a future in the region and proceed with Trump's 20-point plan in Gaza, as well as negotiating the future with Lebanon and other neighbors," the Israeli president said, adding that "Israel needs a stable government that faces these challenges."

Herzog said that he expected Eisenkot to do his best to form a government that would serve all parts of the Israeli people.

In turn, Eisenkot stressed that he is committed to establishing a national emergency government.

"We do not have the privilege of endless rounds of elections. I will send an official approach to all of the Knesset's members, as parties and individuals, for talks," he added.

Eisenkot also addressed Knesset members. "The public looks up to us... We are in the most complicated political situation since Israel's establishment," he said.

What do we know about forming a coalition

Yashar was Israel's second biggest party in Israel's October elections with 21 parliament seats, behind Netanyahu's Likud with 27. However, more members of the Knesset, the Israeli parliament, recommended Eisenkot as the man who should be given the first right to try and secure a government.

In comparison to Eisenkot's 67 recommendations, Netanyahu received the backing of 46 members, with the ultraorthodox Ashkenazi party United Torah Judaism (UTJ) deciding not to make any recommendations despite having joined Netanyahu's governments of the past 17 years.

Should Eisenkot fail to form a coalition, President Isaac Herzog will have the authority to pass the task on to a different Knesset member, with the second person in line expected to be Netanyahu.

If the Likud leader, too, will not manage to form a government, and if no other parliament member will claim to have enough support to head a government, Israel will likely head to another round of elections.

Eisenkot faces a difficult task

Dividing Israel's Zionist parties into blocs results in Netanyahu's religious-nationalist allies receiving 53 seats, with the Eisenkot-led anti-Netanyahu bloc having 48 seats.

Israel's two Arab parties, which with 19 seats received historic support due to the high turnout in Arab and Palestinian communities, already voiced their willingness to support the Zionist opposition in ousting Netanyahu and his government. Mostly the religious Muslim party Ra'am, led by Mansour Abbas, said it is willing to join a coalition once again in a bid to improve Israel's Arab and Palestinian communities' lives.

In 2021, Ra'am made history in becoming the first-ever Arab party to join an Israeli coalition, signing an agreement with right-wing candidate Naftali Bennet and liberal politician Yair Lapid.

The other Arab party, the Joint List, is a union of several smaller parties. While its members have never joined an Israeli coalition, its politicians did provide political support for an Israeli government from the opposition during Yitzhak Rabin's second term as prime minister as his government pushed through the Oslo Accords with the Palestinians, a term which was cut short by Rabin's murder in November 1995.

Campaign promises at risk

Both sides of Israel's Zionist political divide promised not to rely on votes by Arab parties to form a coalition, meaning Eisenkot's bloc will have to track back on one of its election promises to form a government with them.

However, a poll by the Accord Center of the Hebrew University in Jerusalem carried out two days after the elections found that 59 percent of Israel's Zionist opposition voters would rather have a government with Ra'am, and with the Joint List's abstention, than any other alternative.

Another option touted by Israeli media in the past week was the country's two ultraorthodox parties potentially joining an Eisenkot-led coalition. UTJ and Sepharadi party Shas have seven seats each, but a coalition with any of them would require Eisenkot to backtrack on another campaign promise: to pass through a legislation to secure the army conscription of young ultraorthodox men, which the two parties strictly object, citing fears over the future of religious studies in Israel.

Moreover, Shas supporters are known to hold right-wing views favorable to Netanyahu, with party head Arye Deri being considered as one of the politicians closest to Israel's longest-serving prime minister.

Effects on Palestinians

The government formed is bound to have wide-ranging implications on the lives of Palestinians in the Occupied West Bank and the Gaza Strip.

The Netanyahu-led current coalition also includes far-right parties Otzma Yehudit and Religious Zionism, which received 13 seats in the October election. The two parties support annexing the West Bank — a territory illegally occupied by Israel — as well as re-establishing Israeli settlements in the Gaza Strip and carrying out the so-called "wilful migration," the plan to move Gaza's 2.1 million Palestinians to other countries. Large parts of Netanyahu's Likud, too, support the plan.

The two parties often provide political backing to the violent settlers carrying out attacks against Palestinians in the Occupied West Bank.

Eisenkot himself promised to secure a Gaza Strip without Hamas rule within 18 months of becoming prime minister. This stands in contrast to the Netanyahu government's current policy of allowing Hamas to control certain parts of the enclave, despite the US-brokered ceasefire agreement saying a board of technocrats should take over Gaza from Hamas.

While Gadi Eisenkot's bloc includes several right-wing parties, their positions differ from those of Benjamin Netanyahu's coalition. Naftali Bennet, the head of the opposition's second biggest party Beyachad, labels himself as a right-winger and a supporter of settlements.

However, he has repeatedly used strong terms to condemn settler attacks on Palestinians. Eisenkot himself, too, condemned settler violence towards Palestinians, saying they are the result of the Netanyahu government's policies.

entries.title: Iran: US strikes ship after Hormuz blockade breach
entries.summary: The US military said a vessel trying to leave an Iranian port was hit due to the naval blockade on the country. On its part, Iran said three "non compliant" oil tankers caught fire in the Strait of Hormuz.
entries.content:
Middle East

Iran: US strikes ship after Hormuz blockade breach

November 8, 2026

The US military said a vessel trying to leave an Iranian port was hit due to the naval blockade on the country. On its part, Iran said three "non compliant" oil tankers caught fire in the Strait of Hormuz.

The United States struck a commercial ship attempting to breach its naval blockade on Iran, the US military said Sunday.

According to the US Central Command (CENTCOM), the cargo vessel "tried to depart regional waters after visiting an Iranian port," before its stern was struck by "precision munitions" shot from a US military aircraft.

In a video posted by CENTCOM, an explosion can be seen on the M/V Huda's stern as a result of the shooting, with the ship's civilian crew ignoring "repeated warnings."

The authorities in the UAE said 22 people had been rescued due to a fire on a vessel in the Gulf of Oman.

What's the situation in the Strait of Hormuz?

The US naval blockade on Iran, intended to pressure the country into lifting its own blockade on the Strait of Hormuz, has been in force for months.

Iran's own blockade of the waterway, through which a fifth of the world's oil and gas supplies flowed before the war started in late February, saw energy prices spike around the world.

Iran's Revolutionary Guards said three "non-compliant" oil tankers caught fire while going through the Strait. Tehran has regularly attacked vessels going through the Strait of Hormuz without its approval.

Aramco building hit after rocket attack

Elsewhere in the Middle East, the escalation between Iran-backed Houthi rebels in Yemen and Saudi Arabia continued to rage.

Saudi Arabia said it had intercepted incoming missiles shot in the direction of the capital, Riyadh, on Sunday.

Debris from the interception damaged a building belonging to state-owned oil company Aramco. No casualties were reported, but some of the building's floors were heavily damaged, witnesses told AP.

Saudi Arabia accused Yemen-based militant group Houthisof launching two ballistic missiles and two cruise missiles.

While Houthis carried out such attacks in the past, the rebels have not claimed responsibility for the attack yet.

According to the Houthis, 33 people were killed in Saudi-led attacks on Yemen's rebel-held capital, Sanaa, on Saturday.

entries.title: Gaza: Rains add misery to humanitarian catastrophe
entries.summary: With most homes damaged or destroyed by the war, Gazans are facing worsening humanitarian conditions due to heavy rain.
entries.content:
November 8, 2026

With most homes damaged or destroyed by the war, Gazans are facing worsening humanitarian conditions due to heavy rain.

Heavy rains sweeping across parts of the Middle East this week have flooded tens of thousands of tents in Gaza's displaced persons' camps.

According to authorities in the enclave, at least 70,000 tents have been flooded over the past day, where tens of thousands of people took shelter.

No fatalities had been reported, although some people were injured.

Some of the tents have been washed away due to the weather, with mattresses and blankets soaked with water.

Majority of houses destroyed

More than 1.6 million residents of Gaza's 2.1-million population now live in tents or other makeshift shelters due to Israel's war in the enclave.

UN data says some 80% of the enclave's structures have been damaged during the war, with two-thirds destroyed, leaving Gaza's residents — many of whom were displaced multiple times during the war between Israel and Hamas — to either live in tents or risk their lives and seek shelter in buildings that could be on the verge of collapse.

The Higher Presidential Committee for Church Affairs in Palestine released a statement appealing for humanitarian aid for the Gaza Strip due to the situation.

According to the committee, some 950,000 people are living in areas "vulnerable to flooding," with more than 400,000 living in areas of "high levels of risk."

"Heavy rainfall is compounding an already catastrophic humanitarian situation, leaving displaced families and those who have lost their homes exposed to the elements and deprived of the most basic necessities of life," the statement said.

Israel accused of genocide

Some 74,000 people have been killed in the Gaza Strip since October 7, 2023. The war was triggered when Islamist Palestinian organization Hamas and its affiliates launched a terrorist attack in Israel's south, killing some 1,200 Israelis, most of whom were civilians. The militants also kidnapped 251 hostages.

The UN, EU, US and Israel, among others, consider Hamas to be a terrorist organization.

A UN commission of inquiry, as well as many leading human rights organizations, have accused Israel of committing genocide in Gaza. Israel has rejected the accusation, saying its army is acting in accordance with international law.

entries.title: 'Never Again!': Holocaust remembrance under pressure
entries.summary: Only a few Holocaust survivors remain who can share their stories firsthand. Meanwhile, voices calling for an end to what they describe as a "cult of guilt" are growing louder. How can Holocaust remembrance survive?
entries.content:
November 8, 2026

Only a few Holocaust survivors remain who can share their stories firsthand. Meanwhile, voices calling for an end to what they describe as a "cult of guilt" are growing louder. How can Holocaust remembrance survive?

Young people pose inside a crematorium oven at the Buchenwald concentration camp memorial, laughing while they give the Nazi salute and take pictures of each other. "In a sense, they're trophies to post on social media for them to boast about — breaking the ultimate taboo," Jens-Christian Wagner, director of the Buchenwald and Mittelbau-Dora Memorials Foundation, told DW.

"Incidents like this have become more frequent in recent years. We have seen memorial trees planted in honor of concentration camp victims cut down. When something like this happens — and it happens regularly — I find it particularly despicable because, because it ultimately kills these people a second time," added Wagner.

Wagner is part of the curatorial team behind the exhibition "Never Again! Against Forgetting the Crimes of the Nazi Regime" in Bonn's Bundeskunsthalle, or the Art and Exhibition Hall of the Federal Republic of Germany. Wagner said Holocaust remembrance is under pressure, and the subject of intensifying attacks.

Critics have dismissed remembrance as a "cult of guilt" or "national masochism." With right-wing populism on the rise and historical revisionism becoming more common, Wagner worries about how Germany will remember the victims murdered by the Nazi regime. He is also concerned about the future of democracy. And soon, there will be no Holocaust survivors left to tell the true story of what happened.

This new exhibition tackles this concern head-on with numerous works of art and historical artifacts.

Moralizing doesn't help people learn

"I hope that perhaps even some people who don't already believe it's important to confront Nazi crimes will find their way to the exhibition," Wagner said. Memorial sites also attract visitors who aren't necessarily convinced of the need to confront these parts of history. Many of them are students.

"Let's not kid ourselves: When a teacher says 'We're going there,' it's always a mandatory visit," he said.

For today's young people, the Nazi era seems like the distant past, Wagner explained. "When you tell them to remember something that their grandparents didn't even experience, it naturally feels like an emotional burden. They can practically see the finger being wagged at them, and that doesn't exactly encourage learning."

A two-hour lecture won't have much of an impact if pupils aren't even paying attention. Instead, Buchenwald organizes full-day programs that allow students to explore historical sources together and make sense of history for themselves.

The next step, Wagner said, is to show young people that this chapter of history isn't closed. Visitors are encouraged to make connections between the past and current events like migration, for example.

"For the longest time, people have been discussing migration almost exclusively in terms of threats to public safety and crime. This broadly marginalizes certain groups — a mechanism that also worked for National Socialism," he said.

Holocaust survivor: 'The number tattooed on my arm was always there'

Eva Umlauf, 83, knows firsthand what it means to experience exclusion in its most extreme form. She is a patron of the Bonn exhibition.

In November 1944, Umlauf was just 2 years old when she, her pregnant mother and her father were deported by the Nazis from the Novaky labor camp in Slovakia to Auschwitz-Birkenau, the notorious Nazi concentration and extermination camp. She was saved from the gas chambers by mere days; the Nazis stopped using the chambers as the Red Army advanced, hoping to hide evidence of their crimes.

The camp was liberated on January 27, 1945. Three months later, Umlauf's sister Nora was born. But her father, her mother's siblings and her grandparents were all murdered. Eva barely survived herself. She suffered from tuberculosis, rickets and whooping cough, as well as edema caused by starvation. "Forget about the child. She won't survive," a doctor told her mother. But he was wrong.

Her mother returned to what was then Czechoslovakia with her two daughters, settling in Trencin. Eva Umlauf has no conscious memories of Auschwitz, but she carries her family's trauma deep within her.

Her mother never talked about what happened. Even so, Eva knew from an early age that she was a survivor. Her family rarely mentioned the camp by name, but one sentence came up again and again: "They stayed there." Eva knew that meant "they" were dead. And then, there was the number tattooed onto her arm: A26959.

Eva Umlauf: 'I cannot forgive'

Her mother taught her daughters not to draw attention to their Jewish identity — antisemitism was widespread throughout Czechoslovakia at the time. The small family managed to avoid harassment.

Eva Umlauf wanted to become a pediatrician, so she studied medicine. In the 1960s, she met her future husband, Jakob, who had also survived the Holocaust. He was an architect, active in Munich's Jewish community. They married in 1966, and she moved to Germany. She could hardly have imagined that she would one day live in the country of the perpetrators. "I don't hate Germans," she said. "But I cannot forgive. How can you forgive the deaths of 6 million people?"

It wasn't until much later that she first spoke publicly about the horrors of her early childhood. In 2011, she delivered a commemorative speech in Auschwitz on the anniversary of the camp's liberation. Since 2025, she has served as chair of the International Auschwitz Committee. A heart attack in 2014 motivated her to write her first book. "I was in intensive care. I thought to myself: If I get out of here healthy, I'll write a book."

Her memoir, "The Number on Your Forearm is Blue Like Your Eyes," was first released in 2016. The English translation followed in 2024. Since its publication, hardly a day has passed without someone asking Eva Umlauf to share her story.

She is appalled by the disrespectful behavior of young people at former concentration camps and by growing ignorance about the Holocaust. Sometimes, people even ask if she's too old to have a tattoo. But she also recalls a young man on the Munich subway who noticed the number on her arm and told her: "I want to apologize to you for what my ancestors did to you."

'Take care of your country'

Umlauf never imagined that antisemitism would once again become so widespread in Europe and the United States. Nor did she expect the rise of Germany's far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) party.

"I go into schools. I'm so overwhelmed by the number of requests asking for my availability. And yet, the AfD is growing faster than I can reach students. It makes me think all this work is for nothing," she told DW.

Germany must never again fall under a right-wing dictatorship, she stressed. "'Never again' sounds nice, but all I can say is: It's happening again! Wouldn't 'Here We Go Again: Never Again' make a good title for the exhibition?"

She also shared her message to young people in the exhibition catalog, "Never Again": "You are not responsible for the crimes of your grandparents and great-grandparents. But you are responsible for the future. […] You are the generation that will shape our world. Make it a place where everyone can grow up safely, regardless of their background, faith or skin color."

She continues: "You don't have to be perfect. You just have to stay alert. Take care of your country."

The exhibition "Never Again! Against Forgetting the Crimes of the Nazi Regime" in the Bundeskunsthalle in Bonn runs through May 2, 2027.

This article was originally written in German.

entries.title: Poland begins two days of mourning over Krakow shooting
entries.summary: Polish authorities have opened a terror probe after the shooting on Krakow's Main Square. Police confirmed that the bodies found at the suspect's home were those of his parents and sister.
entries.content:
Poland

Poland begins two days of mourning over Krakow shooting

November 8, 2026

Polish authorities have opened a terror probe after the shooting on Krakow's Main Square. Police confirmed that the bodies found at the suspect's home were those of his parents and sister.

Poland began two days of mourning on Sunday, a day after a gunman killed six people and wounded 15 others in Krakow's main market square.

The attack occurred in Main Square (Rynek Glowny) in the Old Town of Poland's second-largest city on Saturday. The area is a popular tourist attraction.

In addition to the six people killed in the square, three bodies found at the suspect's home were the bodies of his sister, mother and father, police said Sunday.

Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk has labeled the attack an act of far-right "terrorism," but authorities have not given a possible motive.

Poland's national prosecutor's office said it had launched an investigation into Saturday's shooting, saying that it constituted a suspected "terrorist offense."

Mourners left candles in the square to pay tribute to the victims of the shooting. Black flags and Polish national flags with black ribbons were also seen in the city.

The square remained partially sealed off on Sunday morning as authorities continued investigations.

What do we know about the shooting in Krakow's Main Square?

The 24-year-old suspect, who was wearing military fatigues at the time of the attack, allegedly shot at people at random as he drove around the square.

He was wounded by police and is in critical condition in hospital.

Polish authorities say the man held right-wing extremist and ultranationalist views.

"Everything indicates that he was fascinated by far-right ideologies," Interior Minister Marcin Kierwinski said at a news conference.

A British national was among the dead, and among the wounded were citizens of Austria, the United Kingdom, Germany, Portugal and Russia, according to authorities.

Two police officers were wounded while confronting the suspect and are in hospital. Officials have launched an appeal for blood donations for one of the officers, who is in critical condition.

The Krakow Carriage Driver's Association told Polish news agency PAP that several horse-drawn carriage drivers were seriously injured in the shooting.

Police confirm three bodies found were members of suspect's family

Police said on Sunday that three bodies found at the suspect's home were those of his sister, mother and father.

The family home is in the town of Ostrowiec Swietokrzyski, around 150 kilometers (93 miles) northeast of Krakow.

Police said that several firearms were seized from the apartment.

The suspect had no previous criminal record, according to Polish media reports.

He and his father were members of a shooting club.
